answer: We obtain \(\displaystyle\int_a^b |f_n(x)-f(x)|\,dx \le \int_a^b \varepsilon\,dx = \varepsilon(b-a)\). The bound \(\varepsilon\) appears because the integrand \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|\) is uniformly bounded by \(\varepsilon\) on the entire interval, so the integral is at most \(\varepsilon\) times the length of the interval.

question: From the definition of uniform absolute‑convergence, explain why the existence of a single \(m\) that works for all \(x\) in the domain is crucial, and how this contrasts with the pointwise convergence condition that would allow \(m\) to depend on \(x\).
answer: Uniform absolute‑convergence requires that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists an \(m\) such that for all \(n\ge m\) and for all \(x\) in the domain, \(|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\). This single \(m\) works uniformly over the whole domain, guaranteeing that the convergence does not depend on the particular point \(x\). In contrast, pointwise convergence would allow a different \(m_x\) for each \(x\), so the bound might fail to hold uniformly across the domain.

Thus \(\bigl|\int_a^b f_n - \int_a^b f\bigr| < \varepsilon(b-a)\). Since \(\varepsilon\) can be made arbitrarily small, the integrals converge. question: Suppose \((f_n)\) is a sequence of continuous functions on \([a,b]\) that converges uniformly to \(f\). question: In the discussion of uniformly convergent sequences of continuously differentiable functions, how does the uniform convergence of the derivatives \(f_n'\) to a function \(g\) lead to the conclusion that the limit function \(f\) satisfies \(f' = g\)?
answer: Because \(f_n'\) converges uniformly to \(g\), for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(N\) such that \(|f_n'(x)-g(x)|<\varepsilon\) for all \(x\in[a,b]\) and \(n\ge N\). Integrating this inequality from \(a\) to \(x\) and using the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(|f_n(x)-f_n(a)-\int_a^x g(t)\,dt|<\varepsilon(b-a)\). Taking limits as \(n\to\infty\) and noting that \(f_n(a)\to f(a)\) yields \(f(x)-f(a)=\int_a^x g(t)\,dt\). Differentiating both sides shows \(f'(x)=g(x)\) for all \(x\).
